name: Amon (son of Manasseh)
title: The Wicked King of Judah
summary: Amon, son of King Manasseh, reigned over Judah for only two years (ca. 642–640 B.C.) after being installed as king at the age of twenty-two. He followed in his father’s early footsteps by worshiping the idols that Manasseh had set up and abandoned the Lord, the God of his fathers. The Books of Chronicles highlight a sharp theological contrast: while Manasseh humbled himself before the Lord toward the end of his life and experienced restoration, Amon refused to humble himself and instead intensified sin. His reign was abruptly ended when his own servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house. However, the people of the land (am ha-arets) crushed the rebellion, punished the conspirators, and installed Amon’s young son Josiah as king—thereby securing the continuity of the Davidic dynasty during a turbulent time. Amon’s short and dark reign forms a grim backdrop for the great reform that his son Josiah later carried out.

keyEvents.title: Amon Becomes King
keyEvents.description: Amon became king over Judah at the age of twenty-two, following the death of his father Manasseh. His mother was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz from Jotbah.

keyEvents.title: Amon's Idolatry
keyEvents.description: Amon did what was evil in the Lord's sight, just as his father Manasseh had done. He worshiped and sacrificed to all the idols his father had made, abandoning the Lord, the God of his ancestors.

keyEvents.title: Amon Does Not Humble Himself Before the Lord
keyEvents.description: Unlike his father Manasseh, who humbled himself before the Lord in his distress and experienced His mercy, Amon did not humble himself. Instead, he increased his sin—a testimony that God's grace must be received personally and cannot be inherited.

keyEvents.title: Amon's Death by Conspiracy
keyEvents.description: Amon's own servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house after only two years of reign.

keyEvents.title: The People of the Land Intervene
keyEvents.description: The people of the land killed all who had conspired against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place, thereby securing the continuation of the Davidic dynasty during a politically turbulent time.

versions.summary: Amon was king of Judah and the son of Manasseh. He reigned for only two years before being murdered by his own servants. He continued in his father's ungodly footsteps by worshiping idols and rejecting the Lord.
versions.title: The Unrighteous King
versions.reason: [major] The Bible mentions Amon's mother by name: Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz from Jotbah (2 Kings 21:19). This should be included.; [minor] Amon's wife Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah from Boshath, is the mother of Josiah (2 Kings 22:1). Although she is not directly named as Amon's wife, this can be inferred. Alternatively, one could leave this blank, but it is worth considering.; [minor] The title 'The Wicked King' is appropriate, but could be made more specific, for example, 'The Wicked King of Judah', to distinguish him from other kings.; [minor] The summary states that Amon continued in his father's wicked footsteps, but it should clarify that Manasseh repented toward the end of his life (2 Chronicles 33:12-13), while Amon did not humble himself before the Lord. This contrast is theologically important and should be made clearer in the summary.; [minor] The list of roles contains only 'king'. One might consider adding 'idolater' or similar to emphasize his spiritual profile, even though 'king' is the primary role.; [minor] The description says that Manasseh 'repented toward the end of his life'. This is correct according to 2 Chronicles 33:12-13, but the contrast is phrased somewhat unclearly. Manasseh humbled himself before the Lord, while Amon, on the contrary, 'made sin even greater' (2 Chronicles 33:23). This could be expressed more clearly.; [major] Footnotes are missing. For a biblical person profile, it is important to include historical, linguistic, or theological notes.

versions.summary: Amon was king of Judah and the son of Manasseh. He became king at twenty-two years old and reigned only two years in Jerusalem (about 642–640 B.C.). He did what was evil in the Lord's sight by worshiping the idols his father had made. Unlike his father Manasseh, who humbled himself before the Lord toward the end of his life, Amon did not humble himself but instead increased his sin even more. He was murdered by his own servants through a conspiracy, but the people of the land struck back against the conspirators and appointed his son Josiah as king.
versions.title: The Wicked King of Judah
versions.reason: [major] According to 2 Kgs 21:19, Amon's mother was named Mesullemet, and Amon's wife was named Jedidah (2 Kgs 22:1 notes that Josiah's mother was named Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath). The Spouse field should be filled in with Jedidah.; [minor] The description states that Amon 'did not walk in the Lord's way', but the biblical text in 2 Chr 33:23 focuses specifically on the contrast between Amon and Manasseh. The wording could be refined slightly to better reflect the biblical text.; [minor] The lifespan '663–640 BC' is based on Amon becoming king at age 22 around 642 BC, meaning he was born around 664 BC. Adjusting it to '664–640 BC' is marginally more precise, but the difference is negligible given the uncertainty.; [minor] The role 'idolater' is descriptive, but one might also consider including 'son of Manasseh' as a contextual marker – however, this is more a relationship than a role, so the current roles are acceptable.; [minor] The summary is good, but could be enriched somewhat by mentioning the theological contrast to Manasseh's repentance and the dynastic significance of the people's intervention more explicitly. It should also be clearly distinguished from the previous version.

footnotes.text: The name Amon (Hebrew: אָמוֹן, ʾĀmôn) can mean 'faithful' or 'craftsman'. Some scholars have suggested a possible connection with the Egyptian god Amun, which may reflect the strong Egyptian cultural influence in Judah at this time, especially during Manasseh's long reign when Assyrian and Egyptian culture shaped the region.

Amon's short reign (c. 642–640 BC) falls within a period of Assyrian dominance under Ashurbanipal. The murder of Amon may have had political motives linked to various factions in Judah—some pro-Assyrian and others seeking greater independence. That 'the people of the land' (am ha-arets) intervened and installed the young Josiah suggests a strong popular movement that sought to preserve the Davidic dynasty.

The expression 'the people of the land' (עַם הָאָרֶץ, am ha-arets) likely refers to the free landowning population in Judah with political influence. This group appears several times in the Books of Kings as defenders of the Davidic dynasty during times of crisis, such as at the fall of Athaliah (2 Kgs 11:14–20).

The account of Amon in Chronicles highlights the contrast to Manasseh's repentance (2 Chr 33:12–13). While Manasseh humbled himself in his distress and experienced God's grace, Amon chose to reject this opportunity and instead intensified his sin. Theologically, this illustrates that God's grace must be received—it cannot be inherited, and a parent's repentance does not guarantee a child's godliness.

According to rabbinic tradition (Sanhedrin 103b), Amon is one of the kings who will have no share in the world to come. The Talmud discusses his wickedness and the fact that, despite having a father who repented, he still chose the path of idolatry. Paradoxically, Manasseh's repentance further underscores Amon's disobedience.

Archaeological finds from seventh-century BC Judah, including seal impressions and bullae, testify to a well-developed administration during this period. Although no artifacts can be directly linked to Amon, they provide an image of the bureaucratic apparatus that functioned under his reign and those of nearby kings.
